title: AQA GCSE Chemistry · Chemistry of the Atmosphere

items.stem: For about how long have the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere been much the same as they are today?

options.text: Around 200 million years
About 4.6 billion years
Some 2.7 billion years
About 1 billion years

items.why: The specification states that for 200 million years the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere have been much the same as they are today.

items.stem: Which gas makes up about four-fifths of today's atmosphere?

options.text: Oxygen, the gas used in breathing
Nitrogen, a very unreactive gas
Carbon dioxide, made in fires
Water vapour, from the seas

items.why: Nitrogen is about four-fifths, approximately 80%, of the atmosphere; being unreactive is why it accumulated and stayed.

items.stem: About what proportion of today's atmosphere is oxygen?

options.text: About four-fifths, roughly 80%
About half of it, roughly 50%
About one-fifth, roughly 20%
Just under 1%, a trace gas

items.why: The specification gives oxygen as about one-fifth, approximately 20%, of the atmosphere.

items.stem: Which of these is present in dry air only in a small proportion?

options.text: Nitrogen, which came from volcanoes
Water vapour, which forms clouds
Oxygen, which algae first made
Argon, one of the noble gases

items.why: The noble gases, mainly argon, are named in the specification among the small proportions of various other gases.

items.stem: Why is the evidence about the Earth's early atmosphere limited?

options.text: Nobody was present at the time to observe what was happening
The time scale of 4.6 billion years has destroyed most of the record
Gases cannot be detected or measured in rock samples at all
The atmosphere has never changed, so there is nothing to look for

items.why: The specification gives the reason directly: evidence for the early atmosphere is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years.

items.stem: Theories about the Earth's early atmosphere have changed and developed over time. What does this best show?

options.text: The scientists who worked earlier must have been careless
A theory that has changed cannot really be trusted now
A theory becomes a proven fact once it has changed
Theories are revised when new evidence becomes available

items.why: Changing in the light of new evidence is how scientific theories develop, and is exactly what the specification describes.

items.stem: According to the theory in the specification, what released the gases that formed the early atmosphere?

options.text: Intense volcanic activity in the first billion years
Photosynthesis carried out by the first algae and plants
Gases brought to the Earth by comets and by meteorites
Carbonates breaking down in the oceans that formed

items.why: The specification states that during the first billion years of the Earth's existence there was intense volcanic activity that released gases forming the early atmosphere.

items.stem: How does this theory explain the formation of the oceans?

options.text: Ice delivered by comets melted on the young Earth surface
Water vapour condensed because the young Earth heated up
Volcanic water vapour condensed as the Earth cooled
Carbonates dissolving in the sea gave the water back

items.why: The specification states that volcanic activity released water vapour that condensed to form the oceans.

items.stem: The early atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today. What does that suggest it contained?

options.text: Mainly oxygen, with only small traces of carbon dioxide
About 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen, just as now
Mainly carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen gas present
Mainly methane and ammonia, with a little nitrogen

items.why: The specification says the early atmosphere may have been like those of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.

items.stem: Where did the nitrogen in the atmosphere come from, according to this theory?

options.text: Volcanoes produced it and it built up gradually
Plants released it during photosynthesis, like oxygen
It was left over when carbon dioxide dissolved
Ammonia in the oceans broke down to give it

items.why: The specification states that volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere.

items.stem: Which two gases may have been present in small proportions in the early atmosphere?

options.text: Methane and oxygen were quite possibly there
Ammonia and chlorine were possibly present
Argon and helium were possibly there
Methane and ammonia were possibly present

items.why: The specification says there may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia.

items.stem: What happened to much of the carbon dioxide once the oceans had formed?

options.text: It was all used up by the algae during photosynthesis instead
It dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated
It escaped into space while the surface of the Earth cooled
It reacted with the nitrogen from volcanoes to make ammonia gas

items.why: The specification states that when the oceans formed carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated producing sediments.

items.stem: What effect did carbon dioxide dissolving in the new oceans have on the atmosphere?

options.text: The carbonates dissolved once more and released the gas
The amount of oxygen in the atmosphere fell sharply
There was no measurable effect on the atmosphere
The amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere was reduced

items.why: Gas that dissolves and is then precipitated as carbonate sediment has left the atmosphere, so the amount of carbon dioxide fell.

items.stem: Rocks about 3 billion years old contain iron minerals that only form when no oxygen is present. Which conclusion does this evidence best support?

options.text: The atmosphere then was mainly oxygen and nitrogen gas
It proves the volcanic theory completely and finally
The atmosphere then contained little or no oxygen gas
Plants must have evolved by 3 billion years ago

items.why: Minerals that form only in the absence of oxygen are evidence that the atmosphere of the time was very low in oxygen.

items.stem: A student is given two different accounts of the Earth's early atmosphere and asked to evaluate them. What is the best approach?

options.text: Accept the later account, as earlier ones must be wrong
Judge how well each one fits the available evidence
Accept whichever account is written in the more detail
Reject both, as 4.6 billion years is far too long

items.why: Evaluation means weighing each account against the evidence and saying how far that evidence supports it.

items.stem: Which word equation represents the photosynthesis that produced the oxygen now in the atmosphere?

options.text: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen
glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water vapour
oxygen + water -> glucose + carbon dioxide gas
carbon dioxide + water -> starch + oxygen gas

items.why: This is the word equation for photosynthesis given in the specification.

items.stem: Which balanced symbol equation represents photosynthesis?

options.text: CO2 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2
CO2 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + O2

items.why: This is the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis given in the specification: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen atoms on each side.

items.stem: When did algae first produce oxygen?

options.text: Roughly 200 million years ago
Some 4.6 billion years ago
About 2.7 billion years ago
About 1 billion years ago

items.why: The specification states that algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago, and that oxygen appeared in the atmosphere soon after.

items.stem: Why were animals able to evolve long after algae first appeared?

options.text: Carbon dioxide rose to the level animals needed
The percentage of oxygen increased gradually
Oxygen reached today's level as soon as algae did
Volcanoes released the oxygen animals need

items.why: Over the billion years after algae appeared, plants evolved and the percentage of oxygen rose gradually to a level that enabled animals to evolve.

items.stem: How did algae and plants change the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: They increased it, as photosynthesis produces it
They had no effect, as they only ever produce oxygen
They decreased it, taking in only that one gas
They decreased it, as photosynthesis uses it up

items.why: Carbon dioxide is a reactant in photosynthesis, so algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

items.stem: Apart from photosynthesis, what else decreased the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: The burning of the fossil fuels that contain carbon in them
The release of nitrogen gas by the first plants and algae
The escape of carbon dioxide gas out into outer space
The formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels holding carbon

items.why: The specification states that carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon.

items.stem: Which sequence describes the main changes in the Earth's atmosphere over time?

options.text: Mainly oxygen at first, then carbon dioxide rising steadily to today
Mainly carbon dioxide, then oxygen rising as carbon dioxide fell
Mainly nitrogen at first, then volcanoes added the oxygen
Almost unchanged since the Earth formed 4.6 billion years ago

items.why: The early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide; the oceans, photosynthesis and the formation of carbon-containing rocks and fuels lowered it while oxygen rose.

items.stem: How were deposits of limestone formed?

options.text: From thick layers of plant material buried in swamps
From plankton buried in mud and heated under pressure
From shells and skeletons deposited on the sea bed
From volcanic ash settling over the ocean floor

items.why: Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the carbonate shells and skeletons of marine organisms, locking carbon out of the atmosphere.

items.stem: How did deposits of crude oil and natural gas form?

options.text: From plankton buried in mud on the sea bed
From trees and ferns buried in ancient swamps on land
From the shells of sea creatures on the sea bed
From volcanic gases trapped deep underground

items.why: Crude oil and natural gas formed from the remains of plankton buried in mud and altered by heat and pressure over millions of years.

items.stem: How were deposits of coal formed?

options.text: From shells and skeletons on the sea bed
From plants buried in swamps with little oxygen
From plankton buried in mud under the sea
From the remains of dinosaurs and land animals

items.why: Coal formed from thick layers of plant material buried in swamps, where the lack of oxygen stopped the plants decaying fully.

items.stem: Which statement about greenhouse gases in the Earth's atmosphere is correct?

options.text: Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane are all greenhouse gases.
Water vapour is a natural gas and so is not a greenhouse gas.
Only gases released by human activity act as greenhouse gases.
Greenhouse gases make up most of the atmosphere by volume.

items.why: These are the three greenhouse gases the specification names.

items.stem: What do greenhouse gases in the atmosphere do for living things on Earth?

options.text: They block the ultraviolet radiation coming from the Sun.
They pollute the air and are harmful to all living things.
They cool the Earth by reflecting sunlight into space.
They keep temperatures on Earth high enough to support life.

items.why: This is exactly what the specification says greenhouse gases maintain.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the greenhouse effect?

options.text: Long wavelength radiation passes through and short wavelength is absorbed.
Greenhouse gases reflect the incoming radiation back down to the ground.
Short wavelength radiation passes through; long wavelength is absorbed.
Greenhouse gases hold warm air near the ground, like a blanket.

items.why: Solar radiation passes through the atmosphere, and the long wavelength radiation emitted by the surface is absorbed by greenhouse gases.

items.stem: Radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the ground. What happens next?

options.text: The ground reflects the radiation back at the same wavelength.
The warmed surface emits longer wavelength radiation.
The surface emits radiation of an even shorter wavelength.
The warm air rises and is trapped by greenhouse gases.

items.why: The Earth's surface, being much cooler than the Sun, radiates at longer wavelengths.

items.stem: What do greenhouse gases do with the long wavelength radiation they absorb?

options.text: They re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards the Earth.
They reflect all of it straight back down to the Earth's surface.
They store it permanently, so the energy never leaves the gas.
They convert it into short wavelength radiation from the Sun.

items.why: Absorption is followed by re-radiation, and the part sent downwards keeps the surface warm.

items.stem: Which human activity increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: Growing rice in fields that are kept flooded all year.
Keeping large herds of cattle on grassland.
Burying more household waste in landfill sites.
Burning fossil fuels in power stations and vehicles.

items.why: Combustion of fossil fuels is a named human source of carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Explain why cutting down large areas of forest increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the air.

options.text: Trees give out carbon dioxide, so cutting them down helps the air.
Cutting the trees down releases the methane that is stored in wood.
Fewer trees are left to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
Losing trees thins the ozone layer and lets more heat in.

items.why: Photosynthesis is the process that takes carbon dioxide out of the air, so removing trees reduces it.

items.stem: Which pair of human activities both increase the amount of methane in the atmosphere?

options.text: Landfill sites and burning of coal.
Cattle farming and rice growing.
Deforestation and cattle farming.
Aerosol sprays and air conditioning.

items.why: Livestock and flooded rice fields are both named methane sources.

items.stem: A student is asked to name two human activities that increase the amount of carbon dioxide. Which pair is correct?

options.text: Burning fossil fuels for electricity, and deforestation.
Cattle farming, and decay of waste in landfill sites.
Burning fossil fuels, and keeping herds of cattle.
Deforestation, and the melting of the polar ice.

items.why: These are the two carbon dioxide activities named in the specification.

items.stem: Which statement best describes what scientists say about human activity and the Earth's temperature?

options.text: Scientists have now proved that human activity is the only possible cause of warming.
Scientists disagree with each other, so there is no reliable evidence at all.
The claim comes from opinions in the media rather than from measured data.
Based on peer-reviewed evidence, many scientists expect the Earth's surface to warm.

items.why: This is the specification's own statement of the scientific position.

items.stem: Why do different climate models give different predictions for future temperatures?

options.text: Climate models are built on opinion rather than on any real measured data.
The temperature of the whole of the atmosphere cannot be measured well.
Global climate is a very complex system, so models must be simplified.
The results of the models have not been checked by peer review.

items.why: The specification says such complex systems are difficult to model, which leads to simplified models.

items.stem: A newspaper article about climate change is described as biased. What does this mean?

options.text: Its thermometers were badly calibrated.
It presents only part of the evidence.
It disagrees with peer-reviewed research.
Its writer is uncertain about the outcome.

items.why: Bias here is selective use of evidence, or opinion presented as evidence.

items.stem: A website claims that the world is cooling, using two years of readings from one weather station. What is the best evaluation of this evidence?

options.text: The sample is too small and the period too short to show a global trend.
The evidence is strong because real temperatures were measured.
The evidence is worthless because a website is not a journal.
Two years is enough if the thermometer was accurate enough.

items.why: A global, long-term claim needs data from many places over many years.

items.stem: Which of these is a genuine uncertainty in the evidence base for global climate change?

options.text: Nobody had measured the temperature of the Earth before the year 2000.
Scientists made mistakes when they recorded their measurements.
It is not known whether carbon dioxide absorbs radiation.
Future emissions are not known, so predictions are given as a range.

items.why: What humans will emit in future is a real unknown, so models give ranges.

items.stem: Why is peer review of climate research important?

options.text: It proves that the conclusions are right and settles the matter for good.
It lets the general public vote on which scientific results to believe.
Other scientists check the methods and conclusions before publication.
It checks that the thermometers were properly calibrated.

items.why: Peer review is checking by other scientists in the same field.

items.stem: Why is a rise of about one degree in the average global temperature important?

options.text: Every place on Earth is now one degree warmer.
It shifts the climate of the whole Earth.
It is too small to change the weather at all.
It shows that the ozone layer is thinning.

items.why: An average across the whole planet moving is a large change to the climate system.

items.stem: Which of these is a potential effect of global climate change?

options.text: Sea level rise, causing flooding of low-lying land.
More acid rain falling on lakes and forests.
A larger hole in the ozone layer each spring.
An increase in deforestation and cattle farming.

items.why: Rising sea level and flooding are named potential effects.

items.stem: Which list contains only potential effects of global climate change?

options.text: Flooding, deforestation, more frequent storms and stronger winds.
Rising sea level, acid rain, changes to rainfall patterns.
Extreme weather, cattle farming, loss of some habitats.
Flooding, more extreme weather, changes to species distribution.

items.why: All three are potential effects the specification expects students to describe.

items.stem: A report says that the risk to a coastal city from climate change is high. What does describing the risk involve?

options.text: How severe the flooding would be, however unlikely it is.
How many people believe that the report is correct.
How likely the flooding is, and how severe it would be.
How likely the flooding is, however small the damage.

items.why: Risk combines the chance of an event with the size of its consequences.

items.stem: What is the carbon footprint of a product?

options.text: Carbon dioxide given off while the product is made.
Greenhouse gases emitted over its full life cycle.
The mass of carbon that the finished object contains.
The carbon dioxide released while the product is used.

items.why: The definition covers carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases across the whole life cycle.

items.stem: Which statement about a carbon footprint is correct?

options.text: It includes methane as well as carbon dioxide, at every stage.
It counts carbon dioxide only, from the factory stage.
It is the carbon locked inside the finished product.
It counts only the gases given off during its transport.

items.why: The definition covers carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, over the full life cycle.

items.stem: A company wants to reduce the carbon footprint of its factory. Which action would do this?

options.text: Fit filters to the chimneys to trap all the carbon dioxide.
Cut emissions only during manufacture.
Make the product from materials containing less carbon.
Take the factory's electricity from wind and solar farms.

items.why: Renewable electricity replaces fossil fuel combustion, so less carbon dioxide is emitted.

items.stem: Which action would reduce emissions of methane?

options.text: Bury much more waste in landfill so that the gas cannot escape.
Fit filters to the power station chimneys to trap the methane.
Collect the gas from landfill sites and burn it as a fuel.
Burn less coal in the power stations that are nearby.

items.why: Capturing the gas stops methane escaping into the atmosphere, and it is put to use as a fuel.

items.stem: Give one reason why actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions may be limited.

options.text: There is no evidence for the warming.
Alternative technologies cost a lot.
Emissions cannot be measured at all today.
The evidence has not yet been peer reviewed.

items.why: Cost is a named reason why action is limited.

items.stem: Climate scientists report their findings to the public, governments and industry, not only in scientific journals. Why does this matter?

options.text: The public can then vote on which findings are true.
It persuades the public to agree with the scientists.
Those groups make decisions that depend on the findings.
Reporting widely proves that the findings are correct.

items.why: Voters, governments and industry cannot act on evidence they never see, so results must reach them as well as other scientists.

items.stem: A monitoring station in a city records carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulates in the air above a busy road. What do these three pollutants have in common?

options.text: All three are released when fuels are burned
All three form from nitrogen in the air
All three come from sulfur in the fuel
All three are gases like carbon monoxide

items.why: The specification names the combustion of fuels as a major source of atmospheric pollutants, and all three of these are released when fuels burn.

items.stem: Which statement best describes what most fuels, including coal, contain?

options.text: Carbon and/or hydrogen, and always a little sulfur
Carbon and/or hydrogen, and possibly some sulfur
Carbon and nitrogen, and possibly some sulfur
Sulfur and oxygen, and possibly some carbon

items.why: This is what the specification states: most fuels, including coal, contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur.

items.stem: A hydrocarbon fuel burns completely in a plentiful supply of air. Which two substances are released?

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water vapour
Sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide and water vapour
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen

items.why: With plenty of air the carbon is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, released as water vapour.

items.stem: Solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons are released from a burning fuel. What do they form in the atmosphere?

options.text: A gas called carbon monoxide
Sulfur dioxide in the air
Carbon dioxide that causes acid rain
Particulates in the air

items.why: The specification states that solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons form particulates in the atmosphere.

items.stem: Petrol is burned inside a car engine and carbon monoxide is found in the exhaust gases. Why is carbon monoxide produced?

options.text: Nitrogen from the air combines with carbon atoms
The oxygen supply is limited, so combustion is incomplete
Sulfur in the petrol takes oxygen from the carbon
The oxygen supply is plentiful, so carbon burns fully

items.why: Inside the engine the air supply is limited, so some carbon is only partly oxidised and carbon monoxide forms instead of carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Oxides of nitrogen are found in the exhaust gases of a hot car engine. Where does the nitrogen in them come from?

options.text: From nitrogen compounds present inside the fuel
From sulfur impurities reacting with hot air
From nitrogen in the air drawn into the engine
From nitrogen given off as the fuel breaks up

items.why: Air is about four-fifths nitrogen, and at the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen from the air.

items.stem: A fuel contains carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur. It is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which products are formed?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen and sulfur dioxide
Carbon monoxide, water and sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide, soot and sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide, water and sulfur dioxide

items.why: With plenty of air the carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide, the hydrogen to water, and the sulfur impurity to sulfur dioxide.

items.stem: A gas heater burns methane in a room where the air vent has been blocked, so the oxygen supply is poor. Which product now appears that would not be formed with plenty of air?

options.text: Carbon monoxide
Nitrogen dioxide
Unburned hydrogen
Sulfur dioxide gas

items.why: With a limited oxygen supply the carbon in the methane is only partly oxidised, so carbon monoxide is formed instead of carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Carbon monoxide leaks from a faulty boiler into a house. Why is this so dangerous?

options.text: It has a sharp smell that people learn to ignore
It turns the water vapour in the room into acid
It is toxic, and colourless and odourless so hard to spot
It is explosive and can set the whole room alight

items.why: The specification states that carbon monoxide is a toxic gas and that it is colourless and odourless, so it is not easily detected.

items.stem: Which pollutants does the specification name as the causes of acid rain?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide
Particulates and oxides of nitrogen
Carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons
Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen

items.why: The specification states that sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans and cause acid rain.

items.stem: As well as causing acid rain, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen affect people directly. What effect on humans does the specification give?

options.text: They cause problems with breathing
They cause dimming of sunlight
They make a hole in the ozone layer
They cause skin damage from sunlight

items.why: The specification states that sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems in humans.

items.stem: Particulates in the atmosphere cause health problems for humans. What other effect does the specification give for particulates?

options.text: They add to global warming
They cause global dimming
They cause acid rain damage
They destroy the ozone layer

items.why: The specification states that particulates cause global dimming and health problems for humans.

items.stem: Particulate levels in the air over a city rise year after year, and less sunlight now reaches the streets. Why do particulates have this effect?

options.text: They are suspended solids that block sunlight
They are a gas that soaks up light and heat
They trap warmth near the Earth's surface
They have thinned the ozone layer above us

items.why: Particulates are tiny solids suspended in the air. They reflect and absorb sunlight on its way in, so less reaches the surface: global dimming.

items.stem: Stonework on a city building is being eaten away, and tests show the rain falling there is acidic. Which rise in air pollution explains this damage?

options.text: More sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
More carbon dioxide from the burning fuel
More carbon monoxide from car exhausts
More particulates from sooty chimneys

items.why: The specification gives sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen as the causes of acid rain, which is what attacks the stonework.

items.stem: A fuel burns with a smoky yellow flame in a limited supply of air and gives off black soot. Why is the soot produced?

options.text: The flame is so hot that it forces carbon out as solid particles
The sulfur in the fuel is left behind as solid soot
The fuel breaks apart into its elements, leaving solid carbon
Not enough oxygen is present to oxidise all the carbon, so some is released as solid particles

items.why: With a limited air supply the combustion is incomplete: there is not enough oxygen to oxidise all the carbon, so some carbon is released as fine solid particles of soot.
